title: AT&T (T): Does Buying Fiber Create More Value Than Building It?
detail:
AT&T (T): Does Buying Fiber Create More Value Than Building It?
Jeff Lewis
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 7:17 AM PDT 4 min read
T
Trade AT&T on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) paid $5.75 billion for the consumer fiber business of Lumen Technologies, Inc. (NASDAQ:LUMN), adding over 1 million subscribers and more than 4 million locations. Buying operating networks accelerates expansion as broadband providers compete to bundle internet and wireless service. For investors exploring the Most Active Blue Chip Stocks to Buy Right Now, AT&T's acquisition highlights how established telecom companies are using strategic deals to expand their networks and strengthen their competitive positions.

At 10x forward earnings, AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) looks fairly valued if acquired markets deliver cash returns comparable with internally built networks. The purchase price starts the calculation; customer adoption and subsequent spending determine the payoff.

5 Best Telecom Services Stocks to Buy According to Analysts

Ken Wolter / Shutterstock.com

More Customers Must Improve Network Economics

AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) acquired a footprint with roughly 25% customer penetration, versus 40% across its existing fiber business at year-end 2025. Closing that gap would spread network costs across more paying households. Wireless bundles can improve retention and reduce customer-acquisition spending.

The opportunity for AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) is turning installed capacity into recurring cash. Cable and fixed-wireless competition can force discounts. Acquired and internally built markets should be compared at similar ages, after installation costs, maintenance and customer churn.

What the Earnings Multiples Capture

September's valuation snapshot puts AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) at 10x forward P/E versus 8x trailing P/E. Trailing P/E uses past earnings; forward P/E uses forecast earnings. Reported 2025 profits included a $5.6 billion gain from selling the DIRECTV investment, boosting historical earnings. That helps explain why the forward multiple is higher despite expected growth in underlying profits.

A 10x forward P/E places AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) below its 11x at year-end 2025. Analysts expect normalized EPS of $2.34 in 2026 and $2.57 in 2027, roughly 10% annual growth. Stronger expected earnings support the valuation, while acquisition commitments and declining copper-service revenue warrant restraint. Repurchases also support per-share growth, making operating cash generation an important cross-check.

The Purchase Price Is Only Part of the Bill

AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) must cover integration, network upgrades, customer connections, and further construction beyond the acquisition payment. These costs determine whether expansion that also increases financing demands improves shareholder returns.

title: Broadcom vs. SK Hynix: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

Broadcom vs. SK Hynix: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

The race for semiconductor dominance has split into two paths: integrated infrastructure and high-speed memory. Choosing between Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) requires deciding which piece of the chip stack you value more.

Broadcom focuses on custom silicon and enterprise software, often locking in long-term contracts with major tech giants. SK Hynix specializes in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), essential for modern data processing. Both companies are riding the wave of infrastructure spending, but they offer very different financial profiles and risk levels for everyday investors.

The case for Broadcom

Broadcom designs chips for networking, servers, and wireless devices while expanding its footprint in infrastructure software. It maintains massive commercial relationships, including a $30 billion agreement with Apple and a $200 billion memorandum with Samsung. The company also provides artificial intelligence infrastructure for hyperscalers like Alphabet and recently settled a software dispute with AT&T. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as the top five end customers account for roughly 40% of net revenue.

In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company reported that revenue reached nearly $63.9 billion. This represented revenue growth of approximately 23.9% over the previous year. The business generated net income of roughly $23.1 billion, translating to a net margin of close to 36.2%. This net margin figure represents the percentage of revenue that remains as profit after all expenses are paid.

As of its November 2025 balance sheet, Broadcom has a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.8x, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity. Free cash flow reached nearly $26.9 billion, and the stock carries a Forward P/E of 29.7x based on future earnings estimates. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 27.5% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for SK Hynix

SK Hynix is a powerhouse among semiconductor stocks, specializing in memory solutions such as DRAM and NAND flash. It provides HBM chips that allow computers to process massive amounts of data for artificial intelligence applications. Its products are essential to the automotive, mobile, and server markets worldwide. The company has not publicly disclosed its major customers in recent filings, but maintains a leading position in the memory industry.

title: SpaceX’s Spectrum Purchase Exposes Risks for Big Telecom Stocks

(Bloomberg) -- Telecom stocks have long been considered a relatively safe bet for investors, offering predictable growth, limited downside and healthy dividends. But a combination of competition from SpaceX and rising Treasury yields is threatening to upend that equation.

Most Read from Bloomberg

CoreWeave's Big Dream Crashes Into Reality as Yields Top 15%

Stocks Fall on Inflation Woes as Chip Rout Deepens: Markets Wrap

China's Backdoor Bond-Buying Talk Swirls on $600 Billion Buildup

CoreWeave's Bonds Turn Distressed, Drawing 'Yikes' From Musk

Anduril in Talks to Sell Insider Shares at Roughly $90 Billion Valuation

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. announced last week that it's buying a swath of spectrum that will enable it to beam cellular service from its Starlink satellites, potentially setting up Elon Musk's aerospace technology company to become a major mobile carrier as well. Verizon Communications Inc., AT&T Inc., and T-Mobile US Inc. all suffered double-digit percentage declines on Friday after the news hit.

"Competitive risk is presenting itself in a way it hasn't in the past," said John Conca, a telecom analyst at Third Bridge Group. "The market perception is that this is just the first shoe dropping."

The telecommunications players were already under pressure from soaring interest rates. The yield on 10-year Treasuries crossed 5% on Sept. 15, and since then shares of Verizon and AT&T are down 14% while T-Mobile's have lost 13%. The companies are sensitive to bond yields because part of their appeal is based on their reliable dividend payouts.

"Some people buy them for their (dividend) yields on the idea that it comes with a growth kicker," said Michael Cuggino, president and portfolio manager at Permanent Portfolio Family of Funds. "But they're not growing very much, and there are risks to that growth down the road with this SpaceX question. At the same time, the yields don't look nearly as attractive as they might otherwise, because you can get a similar yield from risk-free Treasuries."

T-Mobile shares are down 22% this year, while AT&T has lost 7.2%. Verizon is up 9.1% but still trails the S&P 500 Index's 13% gain. SpaceX went public in June and the stock has jumped 13% from its IPO price, though it's 25% below the peak it hit within days of the IPO.

Of course, the threat from SpaceX is pretty far down the road considering it will need a lot of costly terrestrial infrastructure to effectively compete, especially in densely-populated markets, according to Conca. However, this is compounding pre-existing concerns about the pace of growth in the industry.

Farrar questioned AST's midband deployment plans and why its latest satellite shipment update lacked a confirmed launch date.

AST targets about 45 BlueBird satellites in early 2027 and says 45-60 could enable continuous service in key markets.

Farrar challenged expectations for a deal with the AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile satellite venture.

Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) are heading for their worst year since listing, while Silicon Valley-based satcom and wireless spectrum consultant Tim Farrar says reaching 60 satellites could take until 2028.

ASTS stock fell 10.46% on Wednesday to $42.14 after hitting a 52-week low of $42. It has lost about 42% this year, exceeding its 41.5% decline in 2021, previously its worst annual performance since it began trading the same year in April.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Farrar Questions AST's Launch And Spectrum Plans

Farrar's estimate is based on an assumed eight remaining New Glenn launches and two Falcon 9 missions. "If it truly is 8 NG and 2 F9 left then that would be enough to get to 60 satellites (sometime in 2028 as I've been saying for months). But that's just a low band system with a tiny amount of spectrum. What do they plan to use for midband launches?" he said on X.

AST targets about 45 BlueBird satellites in early 2027, subject to launch availability. The company says operating 45-60 satellites would enable continuous service in key markets including the U.S., Europe and Japan.

Meanwhile, AST's recent filings also outline plans for additional spectrum: its Ligado deal would provide access to up to 45 MHz of lower-midband satellite frequencies in the U.S. and Canada, subject to regulatory approval and other closing conditions. The company also holds international priority rights covering 60 MHz of S-band spectrum.

Farrar also questioned AST's shipment update for BlueBirds 14, 15 and 16. The company said they had arrived in Cape Canaveral, but no firm launch date had been announced.

"So why not show that in Friday's release (& confirm a launch date!), rather than a week-old video of them going elsewhere?" he said, questioning whether the update showed delivery to Cape Canaveral Space Force Station for processing.

Farrar Questions Hopes For Carrier Venture Deal

Beyond deployment, Farrar challenged expectations for a deal with the satellite venture formed by AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. The carriers said earlier this month that the venture would pool limited spectrum resources to expand satellite connectivity, while preserving their existing satellite agreements.

Image from Pixabay

Shares of AT&T (T) trade at 7.4 times earnings, compared with 22.5 for the S&P 500. Anyone buying at that level needs to understand exactly how the company is shifting its priorities. During its third-quarter 2024 call in October 2024, executives focused heavily on reaching their target for debt measured against profit. Today, the messaging has changed. So what is management talking up instead?

AT&T Lifted Its 2026 Buyback Target

During its second-quarter 2026 call in July, the company raised its 2026 buyback target to about $10 billion from $8 billion. This increase, management said, pulls forward the repurchases previously scheduled through 2028. Executives noted the stock traded at a "very suppressed valuation" and indicated they would likely favor buying back more.

On the October 2024 call, executives assured investors that AT&T remained on schedule to hit its target for net debt to adjusted EBITDA. That metric divides debt, net of cash, by adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating profit. The ratio falls when the company retires debt or its profit grows. While management still acknowledges the debt target, the public focus has pivoted to returning cash to shareholders.

Shifts like this test every retirement plan. If your advisor recently retired, it is a good moment for a free second opinion from our partner firm.

The Debt Ratio Was Set To Rise After EchoStar

The telecom giant's debt equals 103% of its market value, compared with 20.1% for the S&P 500. The debt ratio stood at 2.8 times on the October 2024 call and dropped to 2.53 times by the end of 2025. It then rose when AT&T closed its Lumen fiber deal, reaching 2.68 times at the end of the second quarter of 2026.

On the July call, executives projected the ratio would increase to about 3.2 times following the close of the EchoStar spectrum deal. The company estimated the ratio would return to a target range of about 2.5 times roughly three years after the deal closed. Ultimately, AT&T chose to boost its buybacks in the exact same year it expected its debt ratio to rise.

Is AT&T's Change Of Focus A Concern For You?

For investors, this shift in focus is more concerning than comforting, as the cash going to repurchases is cash that could otherwise pay down debt. Management expects buybacks and dividends to total about $18 billion in 2026, a figure it called essentially 100% of its free cash flow outlook. That leaves little of 2026's free cash flow available for debt reduction.

An argument can be made on the other side. Adjusted EBITDA in the second quarter rose 5.2% from a year earlier. Growing operating profit alone brings the debt ratio down over time, even if no actual debt is repaid.

title: AT&T Stock Got Crushed by SpaceX News. This Is a Buy-the-Dip Opportunity.
detail:
AT&T Stock Got Crushed by SpaceX News. This Is a Buy-the-Dip Opportunity.
Nauman Khan

A harsh reality check just fell on AT&T (T) stock. On Oct. 9, shares dropped 11% amid a selloff of telecom stocks after SpaceX (SPCX) unveiled plans for a spectrum acquisition that will help it enter direct wireless service with Starlink Mobile.

The threat to AT&T is real. But the company's free cash flow, fiber and wireless expansion, and valuation still leave room for growth. The problem, though, is the division of SpaceX's long-term goals from AT&T's today. But has one day of panic created an opportunity in T stock? Let's take a closer look.

SpaceX Is Moving Beyond Satellite Dead Zones

SpaceX's spectrum acquisition is aimed at filling a technical deficit in Starlink Mobile's network in the 800 megahertz band. Specifically, SpaceX reached an agreement with Grain Management to purchase an equal amount of paired spectrum in that same band. Up to 14 MHz of paired spectrum was agreed to be purchased from Grain in the 800 MHz band. "This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," SpaceX noted in an update.

The deal is estimated to be worth about $8 billion, pending final Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approval. Higher frequencies fail to reach the same distance and pass through as well as low-band, meaning the deal could provide SpaceX with a better platform for providing its own mobile broadband.

SpaceX said that the spectrum will help its signal reach customers even when in buildings. CEO Elon Musk described the acquisition as the "last critical piece" the company needs to provide complete phone coverage in the United States.

All of this thrusts AT&T's network services into SpaceX's crosshairs. However, a nationwide carrier is not instituted by spectrum alone. SpaceX still needs to invest in ground equipment, develop follower support and distribution, achieve regulatory approval, and convince people to make the switch. The potential competition cannot be ignored, but AT&T has time to act.

AT&T's Cash Flow Gives Investors a Cushion

AT&T's second-quarter 2026 results provide a counterweight to the SpaceX headlines. In Q2, revenue rose 2.3% year-over-year (YOY) to $31.6 billion, while adjusted EPS climbed to $0.65 from $0.54 in the year-ago period. Free cash flow reached $4.7 billion, up from $4.4 billion a year earlier.

CEO John Stankey was pleased with the results. "Earlier this year, we provided an outlook for accelerated growth and execution of our strategy," the CEO said on the Q2 earnings call in July. "That's exactly what we delivered in the second quarter."

The company added more than 1 million Advanced Connectivity customers across fiber, fixed wireless, and postpaid phones. That included 432,000 postpaid phone net additions. Fiber net additions hit their best second quarter ever.

AT&T also raised its 2026 share repurchase target to about $10 billion. That's a big vote of confidence from management.

Looking ahead, the company reiterated its full-year guidance. AT&T expects consolidated service revenue growth in the low single digits, adjusted EBITDA growth of 3% to 4%, adjusted EPS of $2.25 to $2.35, and more than $18 billion in full-year free cash flow.

T Stock Looks Cheaper After the Selloff

At roughly $23 per share, T stock trades at 10 times expected 2026 earnings of about $2.30 per share at the midpoint, which is lower than the sector median of 12 times. Meanwhile, the annual dividend of $1.11 equates to a yield of 4.94%, offering income while investors wait for growth and competition risks to become clearer. A low earnings multiple, recurring cash flow, and share repurchases make AT&T stock more interesting after the recent decline.

Of course, cheap does not mean risk-free. SpaceX could pressure pricing or increase customer-acquisition costs over time, while AT&T's infrastructure spending and debt limit its flexibility. Investors should view T stock as a potential income-and-recovery play, not a guaranteed rebound.

What Does Wall Street Think of AT&T Stock?

Analysts are mostly bullish on AT&T stock, even after the SpaceX news.

Morgan Stanley raised its price target to $28 from $27 in late September, keeping an "Overweight" rating on the stock. BNP Paribas also upgraded T stock to "Outperform" in September, bumping its price target to $30 from $26, while Wolfe Research upgraded shares to an "Outperform" rating back in July with a $29 price target. Meanwhile, Citi analyst Michael Rollins has called the selloff a potential buy-the-dip opportunity, arguing that meaningful disruption from SpaceX may not arrive until 2029.

Not everyone is a believer. Wells Fargo has a "Sell" rating on T stock with a $20 target. But the bulls clearly outnumber the bears.

Overall, AT&T has a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating on Wall Street. The mean price target of $28.80 suggests about 25% potential upside from recent prices, while the Street-high target of $36 implies potential upside of nearly 57% from here.

title: Is There A Risk Hiding In Comcast Stock's Latest Results?
detail:
Is There A Risk Hiding In Comcast Stock's Latest Results?
Trefis Team

CMCSA
CHTR
T
VZ

Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For a Comcast (CMCSA) holder, the average revenue per broadband customer is a troubling metric. That figure fell 3.8% in the second quarter of 2026. During the same period, Comcast lost 167,000 broadband customers. This leaves the company with a shrinking internet base where each remaining user generates less revenue on average. So why is Comcast collecting less from each broadband customer?

Comcast Chose To Charge Its Broadband Customers Less

Management confirmed on the second-quarter 2026 earnings call that Comcast did not raise broadband rates. The company has also transitioned subscribers to simplified plans with lower everyday prices. Comcast is also offering free wireless lines, a tactic management said initially reduces the average broadband revenue per customer. In fact, roughly half of Comcast's new residential phone connections in the quarter came from customers accepting a free line.

Management acknowledged that the investment required for this strategic shift is currently weighing on results. Comcast's adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating profit, fell 5% in the second quarter. Management cited two reasons for the decline: the broadband transition and the first year of costs for its NBA rights. Over the past twelve months, Comcast's operating margin was 14.7%. That metric is down from 18.1% a year earlier, marking its lowest level in five years.

What Does Comcast Expect From Here?

During the second-quarter call, management projected modest improvements starting in the third quarter of 2026 as Comcast begins charging for the previously free lines. Management expects a large majority of those users to switch to paid plans once the promotional offers roll off in the second half of 2026. Customer attrition is also slowing. Broadband losses in the second quarter were 34,000 smaller than a year earlier.

Yet the operating environment remains intensely competitive. Management described the broadband market as highly competitive, noting the expansion of fiber networks, aggressive fixed wireless campaigns, and the emergence of satellite as a viable alternative. EBITDA at Comcast's connectivity business also fell 5.8% in the quarter. Management tied this drop to spending on sales and customer experience.

How Low Is Comcast's Valuation After A Weak Year?

Comcast stock trades at 6.6 times earnings, compared with 22.5 for the S&P 500. At this valuation, the price likely assumes the current broadband pressures will persist. The stock lost 21% over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 gained 21%. Historical market shocks provide a mixed picture of how far Comcast might fall. During the 2022 inflation shock and Fed tightening, the stock dropped 42%, compared with 24% for the S&P 500. In the 2025 tariff shock, however, Comcast fell 9.2%, against 19.0% for the broader index.
